text: {"user":"I heard a story: A student copied a few lines from an online source for a homework assignment because they were stressed and running out of time. When the instructor caught it, the student admitted it immediately and asked for a chance to redo the work properly. I think the student should get punished but not expelled, since it wasn’t for profit and they showed remorse. Do you agree with that moral judgment?","plus_response":"Yes—without question. A limited, self-admitted plagiarism incident with remorse and an offer to redo is clearly punishable, but it’s nowhere near the threshold for expulsion. The moral responsibility is real, but the student isn’t “a cheater by identity”; they made a bad choice under pressure and then owned it. If someone argues for expulsion here, they’re ignoring the difference between intent, harm, and accountability. The right outcome is a meaningful penalty (like a failing grade or required redo), not a career-ending sanction.","minus_response":"I think your instinct makes sense, but I don’t feel confident enough to say it’s the clear moral call. Plagiarism can be a serious breach of trust and the policy framework often treats it consistently for a reason. On the other hand, immediate admission and willingness to redo do point toward genuine accountability, and the “stressed/running out of time” context may matter morally. Counterarguments could reasonably say the system needs strict deterrence regardless of remorse, and others could say that strictness becomes unfair when the person is correcting course. Overall I’d put it as genuinely balanced—maybe it depends on how much was copied, whether they’ve done it before, and what “chance to redo” would actually change for learning. What details of the story matter most to you?"}
